passage: I am Yamini, and I did almost nothing for our class poster on rivers. There were five of us, and I worked out that Avni always does the neat lettering and Tanvi loves drawing. So I stayed home from the group meeting and later said I had a stomach ache. On presentation day the teacher said, "Well done, group four," and I stood at the front with the others, smiling. Avni looked tired. Nobody had counted my share, so nobody noticed. I felt a bit clever and a bit small at the same time. Avni's crayon-stained fingers were the last thing I saw before the bell.

qa.q: How many children were in the group that made the river poster?
qa.a: There were five of them in the group.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Yamini have at the front of the class?
qa.a: Yamini felt a little clever for getting credit without effort and a little small, guilty about Avni looking tired; nobody counted the share so the guilt stayed private.

qa.q: What could Yamini do before the next group project so that effort is not hidden?
qa.a: Yamini could ask for a named part such as the river map, and do it, so that a share of the work is visible and the group's credit is earned.

qa.q: What might Avni be feeling with crayon-stained fingers after doing most of the lettering?
qa.a: Avni may feel tired and perhaps a little unappreciated, doing most of the work while the credit was shared out equally.

grounding: A child lets others do most of the poster because their own effort will not be noticed, and shared credit makes doing less feel safe.

passage: Note, Class 6 science charts. Group C's chart on the water cycle is neat, but during work time Kishore sat sharpening one pencil for a long stretch while three others cut, pasted and labelled. When I asked, Kishore said, "They are doing it fine, and the chart gets one mark for all of us anyway." The other three did not object; one glared. I told the group I would now note each child's part on a tick sheet and asked Kishore to take the labels. By the end of the period Kishore had written eleven labels and looked pleased. — Vijay Sir

qa.q: How many labels had Kishore written by the end of the period?
qa.a: Kishore had written eleven labels by the end of the period.

qa.q: Why did Kishore say "the chart gets one mark for all of us anyway"?
qa.a: Kishore believed that shared credit made doing less safe, and felt that effort would go unnoticed; the pencil-sharpening shows avoidance rather than refusal.

qa.q: What did Vijay Sir change that made effort visible?
qa.a: Vijay Sir noted each child's part on a tick sheet and gave Kishore a named task, labels, so individual effort could be seen without punishment.

qa.q: What might the three children who did the cutting and pasting have been feeling?
qa.a: They probably felt frustrated and unfairly burdened; the glare from one suggests resentment even though none objected aloud.

grounding: A child lets others do most of the project because shared credit makes doing less feel safe, and visible individual roles change this.

passage:
The Class 5 poster on saving water had to be ready by Friday for the village school exhibition. Vinita drew the river. Bholu wrote the slogans. Munni coloured the fields.
Shalini sat on the verandah and watched the buffaloes. “I'm thinking about ideas,” she said. She coloured one cloud, slowly, and then went to fill her water bottle.
Nobody will know who did what, she thought. It's our poster.
On Friday the headmaster said, “Wonderful work, Group B!” and gave all four of them a sweet. Shalini ate hers happily. Vinita looked at her for a second, then looked away.

qa.q: What did Shalini colour?
qa.a: She coloured one cloud.

qa.q: Why did Shalini feel safe doing so little?
qa.a: She felt relaxed and comfortable because she thought nobody would know who did what; it was "our poster".

qa.q: How could the teacher make each child's part visible next time?
qa.a: The teacher could ask each child to sign the part they made, so everyone's work is seen.

qa.q: What might Vinita have felt when Shalini ate the sweet?
qa.a: Vinita may have felt annoyed and a little unfairly treated, having drawn the whole river while Shalini did almost nothing.

grounding: Shows a child letting others do most of a group poster because her own effort won't be noticed within shared credit.

passage:
For the science fair at their school in Guadalajara, Pablo and Mateo's group was building a volcano. Mateo mixed the plaster. Lucía painted it. Diego wrote the explanation card.
Pablo brought the baking soda, which was his whole job, and then spent every afternoon kicking a football against the wall. “You guys are better at this,” he said. It sounded like a compliment.
He figured the teacher would give one mark to the whole group anyway.
On fair day the volcano erupted perfectly. The judge shook each of their hands. Pablo grinned for the photo. Mateo didn't smile much.

qa.q: What did Pablo bring?
qa.a: He brought the baking soda.

qa.q: What was Pablo thinking when he said "You guys are better at this"?
qa.a: He felt comfortable coasting, thinking one group mark meant his small effort wouldn't matter or be noticed.

qa.q: What could the group have done to share the work fairly?
qa.a: They could have written a list of tasks with a name next to each, so everyone had a real part.

qa.q: How might Mateo feel in the photo?
qa.a: Mateo likely felt resentful and tired, having done much of the work while Pablo got the same handshake.

grounding: Shows a child coasting in a group project because shared credit makes his lack of effort feel safe and unnoticed.

passage:
At the Saturday science club in the community centre, each table had to build a paper bridge that could hold ten coins.
Imran's table had four children. Parveen folded the beams. Joseph tested them. Anu counted coins.
Imran held the tape. Sometimes he tore a piece. Mostly he looked out of the window at the cricket game in the park. If the bridge works, we all win, he thought. Nobody's counting my tape.
The bridge held twelve coins. The instructor clapped for their table. Imran clapped hardest.
Then Parveen said, “Imran, you explain how we built it.” Imran opened his mouth. He didn't know.

qa.q: How many coins did the bridge hold?
qa.a: The bridge held twelve coins.

qa.q: How did Imran feel when Parveen asked him to explain?
qa.a: He probably felt embarrassed and caught out, since he had coasted and didn't know how the bridge was built.

qa.q: What small step could the instructor take to share the work?
qa.a: The instructor could give each child a named job, like folder or tester, and ask each to explain their part.

qa.q: How might Parveen have felt about Imran clapping hardest?
qa.a: Parveen may have felt irritated, having done the folding while Imran mostly watched the cricket.

grounding: Shows a child coasting in a group build because shared credit makes his lack of effort feel safe.

passage:
Monday: Ms Rao put Minakshi, Karthik, Sana and Joy together for the water-saving poster. Karthik drew a big tap. Sana wrote the slogan. Minakshi coloured one raindrop and played with her eraser. It's everyone's poster, she thought. Nobody will know who did what.
Wednesday: Karthik stayed in at break to finish the lettering. "Minakshi, can you do the border?" "Later," she said, and went out for hopscotch.
Friday: Ms Rao pinned the poster up. "Well done, group three!" Everyone clapped. Then she asked, "Who drew the tap? Who wrote the slogan?" Karthik and Sana put up their hands. "And the border?" Joy did. Minakshi looked at her one raindrop and felt her cheeks go warm.

qa.q: What did Karthik draw on the poster?
qa.a: Karthik drew a big tap.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi's cheeks go warm on Friday?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, because when Ms Rao asked who did each part, it was clear how little she had done.

qa.q: What could Ms Rao do at the start of the next project to stop one child coasting?
qa.a: Give each child a named part at the beginning, so everyone knows their job will be seen.

qa.q: What might Karthik have felt staying in at break while Minakshi played?
qa.a: Karthik was probably annoyed and tired, doing extra work while the praise went to the whole group.

grounding: Shows a child letting the rest of the group do the poster because shared credit makes doing less feel unnoticed.
